title: Nanomechanics of MXene flakes at gold interfaces
authors: Pierluigi Bilotto, Sabine Schwarz, Marko Piljevic, Iago Peters, Michael Stöger-Pollach, Carsten Gachot
abstract: The demand for novel self-powering and sustainable electronics requires major efforts in identifying new advanced materials for nano-applications. MXene have gathered attention due to their electronic and mechanical properties, however, their nanomechanical compliance against a metal-like interface is still not clearly identified. In this work, we employ atomic force microscopy to characterize the nanomechanical properties of a self-assembled thin flake of titanium carbide MXene (Ti3C2Tx) against a gold probe. The investigation returns an interfacial shear stress of 399 MPa, and the observation of nano-wear localized in the center of the MXene flake. Nevertheless, MXene flakes retained their crystallinity in the tribofilms as confirmed by transmission electron microscopy and electron energy loss spectroscopy. The outcomes of this work set the basis for the use of Ti3C2Tx in novel nano harvesting systems involving metal interfaces (e.g., tribovoltaic nanogenerators) with large scope in nanoelectronics, wearable sensing, electric vehicles, and robotics.
summary: This work experimentally investigates the mechanical interaction between MXene flakes and gold surfaces using advanced AFM techniques. The researchers quantified the interfacial shear stress as 399 MPa while confirming that the material maintains its crystalline structure even after undergoing nano-wear. These findings establish a foundation for utilizing MXenes in next-generation self-powering electronic devices.
main_problem: The study aims to characterize the nanomechanical compliance of MXene flakes against a metal-like interface, specifically determining the interfacial shear stress.
main_result: An interfacial shear stress of 399 MPa was measured for $	ext{Ti}_3	ext{C}_2	ext{T}_x$ on gold, and the material retained its crystallinity despite localized nano-wear.
method: Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM), including force spectroscopy and force mapping, was used to measure adhesion forces and derive shear stress. TEM confirmed structural integrity post-testing.
model_or_system: The physical system involves self-assembled $	ext{Ti}_3	ext{C}_2	ext{T}_x$ MXene flakes interacting with a gold probe tip, mimicking metal interfaces for energy harvesting applications.
key_observables: Interfacial shear stress ($	au$), adhesion force ($F_a$), nano-wear patterns, and retained crystallinity in tribofilms.

main_assumptions: The results are highly dependent on the specific metal-MXene interface, and compacting MXenes compromises individual flake tribological behavior.
figures_summary: Figures show AFM topography (including long-term stability), adhesion maps comparing different areas, friction force vs. lateral distance profiles, and TEM/EELS confirming crystallinity and thickness.
paper_structure: The paper systematically uses AFM techniques to map forces and stresses at the MXene/Au interface, followed by structural characterization using TEM/EELS to validate mechanical testing results for applications in nanoelectronics.
why_interesting: While primarily materials science, the quantitative measurement of interfacial stress ($	au$) under controlled nanoscale contact mechanics provides fundamental data on material interfaces relevant to energy transduction mechanisms studied in AMO physics (e.g., Casimir forces, surface interactions).
